utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we are waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom, I'd like to first of all inform the parties that the next witness, who is waiting, will for sure not start his testimony today. So he is -- he doesn't have to wait and find out at 7.00 that he's not needed. So therefore, he can come back tomorrow. Then I'd like to deliver two decisions. The first one is a decision on whether to call Witness 23 for cross-examination and on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for that same witness. On the 11th of July 2007 the Trial Chamber offered to admit into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis the statement of Witness 23 dated the 18th of January 2003. The Prosecution, in its Rule 92 bis application filed on the 19th of February of 2007, had indicated that the witness would be available for cross-examination. The Defence had presumably relied on this assumption in its responses to the Prosecution's application. Before finally deciding to admit the witness's statement, the Trial Chamber therefore requested to the Defence to make submissions on whether cross-examination should be granted. On the 23rd of July, the Defence for Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj filed a request that witness 23 should be made available for cross-examination. The Trial Chamber agrees with the Defence that the evidence of Witness 23 does relate to a critical element of the Prosecution's case, as it concerns the circumstances of the arrest and detention of Witness 6. This is sufficient reason to grant the request for cross-examination of Witness 23. Given the limited scope of her testimony, the Trial Chamber urges the Defence to confine itself to a relatively short amount of time for cross-examination. I now turn to the protective measures requested. On the 30th of July 2007, with a corrigendum filed on the 16th of August 2007, the Prosecution applied for protective measures for this witness. The Prosecution requested that the Trial Chamber allow the witness to retain her pseudonym and to testify with face and voice distortion and that no identifying information of the witness be disclosed to the public. The Defence has not opposed this application. The Trial Chamber has set out the standard to be met for granting protective measures in several decisions and there is no need to repeat it here. Witness 23 has expressed fear for her safety and that of her family, should it become publicly known that she has given evidence for the Prosecution. The witness lives in a small village in Kosovo together with her family. Given the nature of the witness's testimony, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that it may antagonise persons who reside in her community. Therefore, as the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the requirements for granting protective measures are met, it grants the Prosecution's requested measures. In conclusion, Witness 23's statement of the 18th of January 2003 will be admitted into evidence under seal, conditional upon the witness appearing for cross-examination. The redacted witness statement attached to the Prosecution's motion for protective measures will be admitted into evidence under the same exhibit number as the public document at the same time and on the same condition. This concludes the Trial Chamber's decision regarding Witness 23. I add to this decision the following. So what I now say is not part of the decision itself. In the light of the report by a Prosecution investigator, which was annexed to Prosecution's motion of the 30th of July 2007, the Trial Chamber wonders whether a testimony via videolink might not be recommendable for Witness 23. The Trial Chamber would be inclined to grant a corresponding application by the Prosecution, but would like to invite the parties to make submissions before the Chamber will -- would decide on such an application. There is another decision to be delivered but I'll do that at a later stage today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, it's not very polite to ask someone to enter the courtroom and then deal with other matters, but I took the opportunity, since it took a while for you to enter the courtroom, I took the opportunity to deliver a decision which has got nothing to do with you. Then Professor Dunjic, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Emmerson to continue his cross-examination. I'd like to ask you whether you were able to do the homework we asked you to do and whether you identified any in the blue binder, any of the sets relating to a body as potential candidates for being identified as either the two bodies shown on the picture as floating in the concrete part of the canal or the third body of which a photograph was shown to you. Before you answer, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the very beginning of your testimony before the recess. Could you answer my question as far as the homework is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the short time available to me last night and this morning, I was able to analyse these documents and I came to certain conclusions. So if I may, I would like briefly to elaborate on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it goes further than just, "I identified candidates" or "I did not identify candidates." Perhaps then I'll give an opportunity to Mr. Emmerson to elicit these conclusions from you. Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You were about to start summarising the results of the analysis that you've done overnight. Can I ask you, please, just to take it in stages with me? Looking at the photograph behind tab 2 in the blue file, that is D43, can I ask you simply yes or no, did you identify any of the remains beginning with R-18 and concluding with R-35, which could be consistent with the body that we see in light-coloured trousers in photograph D43? Did you identify any remains which you say are consistent with that body from amongst the remains labelled R-18 to R-35?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you please tell us first of all which bodies you say are consistent with the appearance of the body in D43? Give us the list of bodies you say are consistent.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I in fact wanted to start with this photograph. I first analysed the photograph in order to be able to establish which bodies are consistent with it. The photograph that you mentioned, we see that the body is that of an adult, most probably a male, in light-coloured trousers. But the quality of the photograph submitted here is of a lesser quality so that it is not possible to distinguish any particular details. However, we can see that they are male trousers with a belt and that the right-hand trouser leg appears to be more submerged in water so that it has turned a darker grey, whereas on top, there is something that looks like red clothing and pieces of clothing that seem to be pulled over the head and on both arms. The body is turned so that the legs are going downstream. On the photograph, we cannot see the degree of putrefaction so it is not possible to compare with reliability with what we found upon the post mortem of bodies. However, if this photograph is looked at more closely - and could it be shown, please - in the waist area between the top part and the lower part of the body, there seems to be a kind of split in the left-hand side of the body, as if the top is separated from the bottom partially. Having analysed the bodies in the canal, there are two persons that could possibly correspond to the body shown on the photograph. And those are R-21 and R-24, where we can see a separation of the body and R-29. Now, why am I saying that there are two possibilities? One possibility is the person marked -- labelled R-29, and when I looked closely at the description of the clothing, I saw that it was a male between 23 and 27 years of age, and about 174 centimetres in height, which would correspond to this body in the canal and what is most important is that this person had a red shirt taken off the body. As for persons 21 and 24, they would be consistent in terms of the position of the body. The lower part of the body, wearing trousers, which on the attached photograph in the blue binder, it is R-24. When you look at this photograph you will see that the trousers are light in colour. I won't say white but light in colour. And when those-- when that body was brought for the post mortem, for the autopsy, and when the clothing was washed, we found that these were not white trousers but darker-coloured trousers. Why am I emphasising this? Because the photographs made here, as photocopies of the original photographs that I supplied, differ amongst themselves, and this white colour doesn't mean that the material was white. During the drying of dirty clothing, it appears to be whitish but, in fact, it is a layer of mud or whatever which dries in the sun and gives this impression. So to conclude, on the basis of my analysis, this first body that you mention seen in the canal, could correspond to the bodies marked R-29 or R-24 or 21 and 24, the top and bottom part of the corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if I can look at that with you just briefly. R-21 and R-24, just to be clear, they are respectively the lower and upper part of the same human body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if we look behind tab 21(D), we can see at the bottom photograph the state of the clothing that was found; is that right, on the upper part?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And your suggestion is that those items of clothing that we see there are consistent potentially with the appearance of the body that we see in photograph behind tab 2, that is to say photograph D43? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The photograph showing the clothing taken off the upper part of the body is very poor and very dark, so that one cannot see properly. It is possible that a part of the clothing, for instance this blouse, could have been over the head and over the arms, as it appears on the photograph. But this dark red T-shirt was not identified. I just said that this was a possibility because the body was cut in half. The other possibility, which in my view is more probable, is R-24, which does have this -- I'm sorry, R-29, which does wear this dark red T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We will come to R-29 in a minute, Mr. Dunjic. You've offered us two possibilities and I'm wanting to explore the first one you've offered us which is R-21 and R-24. Now, just to be absolutely clear and you have the post mortem report there for the upper part of the body, R-21, which in the B/C/S is tab (G) there, behind 21, and at paragraph 7, you have recorded, not that the clothing was found nearby or separated from the body but that the bones of the body were found inside a dark blue woolen suit jacket with pockets on the outside, with tiny stripes and a black silky lining, without any size label with blue buttons and a long-sleeved brown shirt with white buttons. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear in the last sentence of paragraph 1 of the post mortem report on R-21, it's perfectly clear that the upper part of the body was found inside those clothes, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you still say that it's a possibility that R-21 and R-24 is the body shown in the photograph D43?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to point out once again that I analysed both the upper and lower part of the body. In the lower part of the body, and judging by the colour of the trousers, this could be consistent with that body, in terms of the body, build, the length, the age also, but the clothing found on the upper part of the body could have included a shirt and the jacket could have been thrown over the head and the arms. When we put the body on the table, we described what we found on the body. But not the position of each piece of clothing, which is rarely done unless the clothing is removed. So in a sense, the body, R-21 and R-24, judging by certain elements and the clothing, could be consistent but I can't be explicit about that. I can't be absolutely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And if we look behind tab (J) there, you'll find the post mortem report for the bottom half of the body, again just so that we are clear, the reference there is to the fact that the bones of the body were found inside dark blue woolen trousers with diagonal pockets on the side and a small pocket below the belt on the right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, to avoid whatever confusion for the witness, I think it's (H) for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry in the B/C/S version, yes, Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, the outer clothing on the bottom half of the body was dark blue woolen trousers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to ask you to look again at the photographs of those clothes under (F). And you will see that those trousers, which are described as being dark coloured, for the purpose of identification, which we tried to do using the clothing, we can see that it is partly dark and partly light in colour, and if you see that and compare it with the photograph we are talking about, the photograph of the canal, you will see that it is very similar. I'm sure you will agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not for me to agree or disagree with you, Mr. Dunjic. Looking back at D43, the photograph of the body floating in the canal you can see very clearly a dark belt, can't you, in contrast to the colour of the trousers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic said already that he identified -- he said already that there was a belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The point I was seeking to draw attention to was the contrast.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you look at the photograph D43, Mr. Dunjic, to your left there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The photograph. Yes. It's very easy to discern the difference in colour, would you agree, between the black belt and the light-coloured trousers, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you help us with this? The state of decomposition of R-21 and R-24 was, I think you've recorded it as being advanced putrefaction, decomposition and skeletalisation, most of it without soft tissue; is that a correct summary in relation to R-21?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the upper part of the body. R-21 is the upper part of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that and in respect of both the upper and lower part of the body have you recorded advanced putrefaction, decomposition and skeletalisation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that most of the remains were without soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just turn then to R-29 for a moment, please? Again we have the photograph of R-29 in situ behind tab 29(A). Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think at the bottom right-hand corner of the photograph, we can see part of the exposed bone as it appeared in situ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that that state of decomposition that we see in the photograph at 29(A), with the bare bone exposed, is consistent with the photograph at D43?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be consistent because, on photograph D43, we cannot see the condition of the legs beneath the trousers, whether there is any soft tissue or not and to what extent it has been decomposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if you just like to, with D43 in mind, if you'd just like to turn over to the photographs at 29(B) where we can see the body laid out, if you could just look at the middle photograph there, is that a photograph -- just so that we are clear, the bones that we can see in the centre of that photograph, is that the bones of a hand?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. What are we looking at there, with the central portion of bone there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central portion are parts of ribs, part of the skull, and these long bones are part of the upper and lower leg. In the case of this photograph, I would kindly ask for the possibility to comment on it, because I have noticed on other photographs as well that the bodies found in the earthen part of the canal and generally next to the canal, are bodies that were in various stages of putrefaction and decomposition, and during the exhumation or, rather, the removal of those bones from the location, we put them in those plastic black bags, in view of the lie of the land, the steepness of the slope, et cetera, it was usually two or three and even four men who would carry the remains in those plastic bags. And we didn't use stretchers all the time for pulling out the bodies from these rather inaccessible areas, and this resulted in these bones being in a pile like they are on this photograph, and mixed together, and I wish to draw your attention to this fact, and that it should be understood in this way because the bones were partially separated and partially linked by soft tissue and they couldn't be lined up anatomically as we usually do. But the photographs were made to prove that those were bones taken from that location and with that number. As soon as the bag was opened, and in later stages of our work, we would position the body anatomically, in the physiological position. So there is a distinction. I want to make this clear so that no one should think that these are two different bodies. The fact that the plastic bag was carried containing a mixture of bones and tissue produced this kind of photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No one is suggesting these are two different bodies. If you could just bear with me for a moment. First of all, and I'm looking at post mortem report, paragraph 1, now, which you will find behind tab 29(D) in B/C/S and we have behind tab 29(E) in English, can you confirm that the remains as you examined them were in a state of almost complete skeletalisation with no soft tissue so that the bones were bare and dislocated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the soft tissue was missing. However, there were parts of soft tissue that were preserved and they were mixed with mud and dirt from the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. But again, just so that we are absolutely clear because you've been asked to do this overnight, you say that photograph D43 is consistent with a set of remains on which there was no soft tissue so that the bones were bare, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were bare subsequently, but what was interesting for me on this photograph, and on this person from the canal, was that the red, dark red shirt was found. It was the only body with such a coloured shirt, and it was a male corpse. This was the link we managed to establish in order to tie these two things together, this body and the clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again, just so that we are clear, the shoe that you see on the foot in the body in photograph D43, if you could just look at the photograph again.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The photograph?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. On the right foot there is a shoe; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. There is some footwear there but as to whether it was a shoe or a sneaker, I cannot tell by this photograph alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And found with R-29 was a black training shoe; is that correct, and a blue blazer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was found were sneakers, Adidas sneakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they were black in colour, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Black sneakers with three white stripes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And a bluish tweed blazer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please have the comparisons that you suggest could be made for the other two bodies we see in the photographs? I won't go in the same level of detail in cross-examination with you about those but perhaps you could just help us, please, first of all, as to which body you say is consistent with the photograph we see behind tab 3, that is photograph D44.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this photograph, well, what we have there are two, not three, bodies. One is 43 and this one is 44 if I'm not mistaken. There are only two corpses in the canal there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you about another corpse in a moment.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like us yet again to go over what I was able to analyse by looking at these photographs. We can see here a body which for the most part is naked and in its upper half or rather the arms, the neck and the head, there is some sort of cloth there which seems to be of light colour, with some green, if I can see this clearly, but I do have to say that yet again this is a poor quality photograph. It does not reflect the true colour contained in the originals. In the lower part of the body, from the lower part of the upper leg downwards, there is a piece of cloth as well, but the rest of the body was naked. Judging by the size of the bottom, it is very likely to be correct, I would say that this was a female. When analysing all of the bodies found.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you just pause there? Yesterday you told us that it was the body of a male and indeed you said that to the Prosecution when they interviewed you about this earlier in July. Have you revised your opinion now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, yesterday I said that it was possible that this was a female body. I never stated absolutely that this was a male body. I said that there was a possibility that this was a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll check your transcript from yesterday, Professor Dunjic. Carry on then, please, if you will. Which body do you say this is consistent with?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I'd like to continue. Upon analysing this in more detail, I was able to establish another possibility judging on or by what I saw here. There are several things here that prompted me to think that this person in the canal, that the bodily remains there, may belong to R-32. Since this was a stout person and I believe it was a lady who had-- just one moment, please. Who was between 18 and 22 years of age, around 170 centimetres tall, rather heavily built. And this is what I could conclude concerning the corpse shown on the photograph. The part of the skull bearing the mark 18/1 was found just below the natural waterfall, next to the car there. This tallies or rather this corresponds to the rest of the skull that was found with the rest of the body further downstream toward Radonjic Lake. In analysing all this, I concluded that this body must have fallen in the area of the waterfall and that a part of the skull remained there whereas the rest of the body floated downstream. This person for whom I believe or suppose that may correspond to the person from the canal, wore blue-green woolen pants -- sorry, sorry, that's another person. I apologise. If I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the body R-32 is naked.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, she had no clothing. In the autopsy photographs, since I studied those as well, one can see part of the body in the middle photograph in annex C. Well, we can see here that we managed to establish an entry-exit wound but there are also parts of tissue there that according to the degree of putrefaction may correspond to the person in the photograph, R-44, if I'm not mistaken. That is why, upon analysing these photographs, I made that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And finally, are there any other bodies that you say could be consistent with that photograph, R-44 [sic]? I'm sorry, may I just correct the transcript, it's D44, not R-44.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I analysed the rest of the bodies too. The only body that could fit the description, according to some of the characteristics, was this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Finally, can I ask you, please, I'm going to, in a short while, play a very short passage of video after the next break just to invite you to comment on the position of the bodies in the video of the canal section. But can I ask you finally in this section of questions to tell us which bodies, if any, you say are consistent with the bodies shown in the photographs behind tab 4(A) and (B) which at the moment do not have an exhibit number but are respectively (A), document 1D53-0448 which is also 65 ter number 871, page 31, and (B), document 1D53-0449. Looking at the photographs behind tab 4(A) and (B), Mr. Dunjic, can you help us as to that body and any bodies that you say are potentially consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs were taken without having assigned numbers to them. Therefore, I presume that this body was marked later and that it had been photographed before that. Therefore, I cannot link any of these photographs to any particular body number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I understand that you're not in a position to make a positive identification but as with the other two bodies you've been invited overnight to consider which of the bodies marked 4(A) and 4(B) are consistent with.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I thought I needn't analyse these bodies as well, on top of those found in the canal. I was told to check whether these -- or which of the two bodies from the concrete part of the canal could correspond to the bodies found in the earthen part of the canal. Another thing I was supposed to do, in my understanding, was to see whether there were any other bodies according to (redacted) testimony, was 80 degrees burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, the analysis of 4(A) and (B) was not conducted, since I had no parameters for that. First of all, I don't know where they were taken and when the body that was found was actually pulled out and marked. I can say that outright. We can see here an upper part of the body whereas in the other photographs we have lower parts of bodies which may correspond to some other corpses that were subsequently found. I solely analysed the two corpses that I was tasked with, the ones pertaining to the concrete part of the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may be that there was some misunderstanding in the questions that you were asked to address your mind to overnight. You did understand you were being asked as well to look at the remains that were recovered from R-18 onwards and to assist us to identify, if you would, please, whether there is any set of remains that is consistent with the passage that I put to you from the statement of (redacted), this was paragraphs 24 and 5, and 32 and 33, where he describes an 80 per cent burnt male body that was found two to three metres from the up-turned car and recovered with the assistance of the fire brigade. Were you able to assist in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please look at photograph 18(A) and 18(B)? In these two photographs, one can see the upturned vehicle. Behind the rear part of the vehicle, it seems the trunk lid is open and we can see there some bodily remains. Parts of the body. In photograph 18(B), one can see the body shot from a different angle. It is charred along its entire back side and it was the only body that was burned. If we take a look at his statement, what I believe he remembers is this photograph, 18(B), where we can see that the body had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We are obviously not asking you to explain what (redacted) might remember but he's recorded in his witness statement there being two separate bodies, one male and one female, who were burned, the male being 80 per cent burned and being found two to three metres from the car, as well as the female. And as I've understood your testimony, never mind what you think he might be -- the reasons he might be mistaken, if I've understood your testimony correctly, your evidence is that there was only one such body and that was the body of a female?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now, if I may, please, to the point at which we left off yesterday afternoon when I was asking you some questions about the estimation of dates of death. And I asked you in particular about bodies R-14 and R-15, and I just want to make sure I've understood your evidence correctly in relation to R-14 and I'm referring here to transcript 7271, lines 10 to 14, from yesterday. You said to us yesterday, "My impression was that this person, R-14, the body was decomposed to a greater degree and that is the reason that I gave this time frame." You'll recall you gave a time frame of April or May. And you went on to say, "I cannot be specific and claim this because this could have occurred also in June or July." Now, I just want to understand. When you've given these estimates, then, you accept that you could be out by as much as two or three months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is only an estimate when assessing such putrefied bodies. That is why I allowed for such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, and in asking questions using the expression "margin of error," I hope I don't cause any misunderstanding here, but what I'm interested in exploring with you is the extent to which you accept that your estimates may be wrong. Now, I'm asking you these questions because I want specifically to ask you about bodies that were allegedly recovered from the area around the economic farm after you had left the scene. And you know the bodies I'm referring to, the ones that were ultimately labelled Re-2 to Re-6. Now, first of all, we have heard testimony from a police officer called Radovan Zlatkovic who states that he was present when the bodies that were labelled Re-2 and Re-3 were found. And if you could just look at the brown file for a moment, tabs 37 and 38, where there are photographs that the witness there referred to -- again, I may have given you the wrong reference. It may be the yellow file. Just bear with me for one moment. Yes, I'm sorry, it is 37 and 38. Do you see those pictures?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And my first question is simply to invite you to confirm, please, we have heard testimony from Mr. Zlatkovic that there was a member of the Belgrade forensic team present at the site when those two bodies were in situ and before they were removed. And I'd like to start if I may by asking you to confirm that that is not correct, there was no member of the Belgrade forensic team present at the time when any of the remains, Re-2 to Re-6 were in situ.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I can confirm that no one from our team was there. The bodies had been transferred there and the next day when we came to the scene we conducted an on-site investigation to see whether apart from the bodies found there, there were any other traces, and we tried to see what the context, what the circumstances, under which the bodies had been found were, whether there was any water nearby, marshes or anything of the sort. The next day upon our arrival, we found parts of tissue, which confirmed to us that indeed there had been bodies lying there and that these bodies were later moved to Pristina -- sorry, to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, with each of these bodies, and for this purpose I'm including Re-1, all the way through to Re-7, with each of these bodies, in your statement, you have given an estimated time of death as July or August, and just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Having regard to the evidence that you've already given, I want to put certain dates to you and to ask you whether the dates that I am putting to you are consistent with what you observed. Now, as far as Re-1 is concerned, we have material before the Trial Chamber in the form of a statement from the wife of the individual who was identified by DNA as Re-1 indicating the 30th of August as the date that that individual was last seen alive, and I imagine you in respect of that body would agree that what you saw was consistent with that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With Re-2 and -3, there is a similar date which has been provided to the Prosecution by the son of the individuals who were identified as Re-2 and -3, to the effects that they were last seen alive on the 6th of September. Would you accept that the state of what you observed is consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the benefit -- and I'm not sure whether you've seen it yet -- but we have the benefit of the second opinion report that the Prosecution have commissioned from a team of French pathologists led by a lady called Professor Dominique Lecomte. Is that a report that's ever been shown to you at any time? No?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to take you to the substance of it at this point. But Professor Lecomte's estimation in respect of Re-2 and -3 is that they had been dead for a minimum of eight and a maximum of 15 days. Again, is that a margin of error that you're prepared to accept on your own estimations of July and August?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My estimate is broader, and with all due respect for my colleagues, I must say that the degree of putrefaction -- that such a degree of putrefaction corresponds to a time of death being at the end of August, and possibly beginning of September. So it can be accepted. But what I must point out, on the basis of my enormous experience, unfortunately, with this kind of work, this degree of putrefaction can be seen very briefly under certain conditions that the body is found in after death. I have seen similar changes even five days after death in an apartment, and also two months after death. So because I provide such estimations for the Court, I give a maximum time frame for this estimation. Now, if you now show me a document which explicitly establishes that that person was seen alive for the last time on the 5th of September, then I can say it is consistent with my finding, but if you tell me that that person was seen on the 5th August, then again, under certain circumstances, depending on the weather, whether it was hot or cold, whether the body was under cover or not, this could also be consistent. So that is what forensic medicine does.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what I have established is consistent with the report you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll just be clear about that. I'm not sure that it is consistent, Mr. Dunjic. Are you saying that when Professor Lecomte says that the state of the remains is consistent with death having occurred between eight and 15 days prior to recovery, which would put it at somewhere between the 8th and the 15th of September, are you saying that that is an opinion that you can or cannot accept as being correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I remember very well that during Mr. Dunjic's testimony as well as the other forensic expert, the Defence in the name of Mr. Dixon, did not wish this report to be provided to Mr. Dunjic so that he could make -- that he could comment it. He is being shown a number of findings today, findings made by Professor Le Compte, and I think if we needed detailed explanations on the parts of Mr. Dunjic, I think he should be allowed to be able to read this report and look into the details of it more specifically dates of death, which are always complex issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have certainly no difficulty in Dr. Dunjic looking at the report. It's in the green file behind tab 13. The reason why I'm dealing with it in the way I am is essentially to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think perhaps the matter could be approached in the following way. What, as far as I understand, you're trying to find out, to what extent the findings of Dr. Dunjic are incompatible with the findings of Professor Lecomte. Now, there are -- I think there are three things that could be relatively easy to be explored. That is to whether on the basis of the findings of Professor Dunjic, the minimum time expressed by Professor Lecomte is criticised by him because on the basis of what he found he would not agree with the minimum. Then as far as the maximum time is concerned, it seems that Professor Dunjic gives a rather broader time frame, whether he would criticise that, and if there would be a difference of view on the matter, then of course the next question would be what elements have been taken into consideration by Professor Dunjic and what element have been taken into consideration by Professor Le Compte, in order to find out whether they based their conclusions on any different sets of data. I think that's the approach which I recommend you to follow and to see whether the next step would still be necessary if the previous step has been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very happy to deal with it in that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Taking bodies Re-2 and Re-3, just to reminds you what the position is, you've agreed I think with the suggestion that what you observed could be consistent with the reported date of disappearance of the 6th of September. Now, Professor Lecomte's estimate, based on what she observed, is that those two bodies had been dead at the time of their recovery for between 8 and 15 days which would put the earliest date of death at about the 8th of September and the latest date of death at about the 15th of September. Now, with that framework in mind, first of all, do you accept that they could have been dead for as little as eight days? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to give you a straight answer, Your Honour, because again this is a time frame of two weeks. Changes can be of this kind too but I would be more inclined to give the date between the 31st of August and the 6th of September. So that -- in such a period of time, it is possible to see such a degree of putrefaction. I have every respect for what my learned colleague said, but on the basis of my experience, because I have examined a large number of corpses, and I know that there are different rates at which putrefaction occurs. For instance, in order to clarify what I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before you go into a full explanation, your opinion is, and in respect of these two corpses, that you do not believe that they could have been in the state of putrefaction that they appeared to be if they had only been dead for eight days? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so far as the outer limit that Professor Lecomte gives of 15 days, I presume from the evidence you have already given that you would say that you disagree with that also because in your view they must have been or could have been dead for considerably longer than 15 days, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My answer is that this 15-day period is more acceptable on the basis of my own experience, but I do allow for the possibility that it could have been longer and that is why I said July and August, because putrefaction has different degrees and rates. If I were to judge what my colleague said, then it would be more acceptable to say that death occurred 15 days prior to recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands whether at this point further clarification of the answer is required. I would otherwise move to the next body and do it reasonably briefly in the same formulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think with a statement -- with the testimony saying that it's very probable or there is a fair chance that the person died 15 days before it was examined, I take it, Professor Dunjic? 15 days before the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before it was discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see it when it was discovered? Because we have a date of discovery and we had a date of autopsy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of autopsy is two days later, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the 15 days, are you talking about 15 days prior to the date of the autopsy or 15 days prior to the date of discovery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have been shown the photograph in situ of the body, so 15 days before the body was discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings us to the 8th of September. And would you like to bring, if you say 15 days is, as I understand, is what you consider a fair possibility, could that be one or two days less, three days less? Could it also be a couple of days or a week or two week more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the professor who gave an estimation of seven to 15 days would also agree with this possibility. It is not possible to determine the date of death with precision to the day. We need some other relevant data such as the statement when the victim was seen for the last time. So it doesn't mean that the victim died on the 8th of September. That victim could have died three days before and even 10 days before, and to have the same kind of changes on the body. But it could also be on the 10th and the 11th of September. So this is the time frame that we accept as forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think then the matter has been sufficiently explored. Nevertheless, Professor Dunjic, if you allow me one observation, your expertise, I think, is the examination of remains and draw conclusions on the basis of that expertise of your specific skills and your specific experience in that field. Now, to include into such conclusions any statements perhaps given by someone when a person was seen last, I think that's outside your expertise because it requires an assessment of the reliability of such statements, and it brings the matters into a broader context, which, where judges are perhaps not experts in your field, of course, judges are experienced and are trained for drawing conclusions from several sources. So may I invite you that whenever you include in any of your conclusions any element foreign to the core of your expertise, such as information you may have received about people having been seen last or reports on people going missing, to explicitly tell us that that is part of what you considered when drawing conclusions? Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I indicate in the light of the way that the questions and answers have progressed and the answers in particular the witness has given, I wouldn't propose to repeat the exercise unnecessarily with Re-4 and Re-6 where the reported dates of disappearance are the 4th and 6th of September which appear to fall within the parameters that the witness has already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could perhaps put it very general question in that respect on whether what he just told us about R-2 and R-3 whether that would ask for any different consideration if Professor Lecomte would have come to similar conclusions in respect of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way, Mr. Dunjic. In respect in particular of R-4 and R-6?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Isn't it Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Re-4 and Re-6,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made that mistake first.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We have reported dates of disappearance of the 4th and the 6th of September respectively and as I understand the evidence that you've already given in respect of Re-2 and -3, unless there is any different factor at play, you would accept that the appearance of the remains that you saw would be consistent with deaths occurring after the 4th of -- or 6th of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two things I'd like to mention. I'd like to indicate that on page 28, lines 6, R-2 and R-3 are mentioned. I think we should read Re-2 and Re-3. Second point, I would like to recall that these bodies Re-4 and Re-6 are not included in the indictment. This is why I wonder how relevant these questions are, given that these are not charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the first matter is clear, corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would hope I've made it sufficiently clear in the way that the case has been presented from the outset that the Defence are interested in the origin of those remains and why it is that the Prosecution has removed them from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without giving any evaluation of the relevance of that, it could not be considered not relevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just repeat the question to you and I'm taking it shortly with you, Mr. Dunjic. In respect of Re-4, we have a last-seen-alive date of the 4th of September, in the evidence and in respect of Re-6 we have a last-seen-alive date of the 6th of September. I think you've already accepted in respect of Re-3 and -4 that the observations that you made are capable of being consistent with the disappearance on the 6th of September. So do I assume in relation to Re-4 and Re-6 that they too would be consistent with those individuals having met their deaths on or after the 4th and 6th of September respectively?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as in the previous case, and as an expert I would never stick firmly to such dates, 15 days, seven days and so on. I always endeavour to provide a broader time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And similarly, would your answers be the same in respect of Professor Lecomte's opinion relating to those two sets of remains that they are between eight and 15 days old? Would your response be the same in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the same, only one can see it is more than 15 days from the day of discovery, so it's the 16th, 17th or 18th. One should not stick firmly to 15 days and not a single day more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Obviously, that's an issue that Professor Lecomte will want to explore. I want to come to one other aspect of her report with you very briefly. You gave evidence when you were giving evidence-in-chief, and this is transcript 6828, line 7, that in your opinion, the bodies had been in situ for a long time, and I think in your statement you suggest that the bodies that you saw by the side of the canal had been there for at least one and a half months. What I want to do with you, please, is just briefly explore the possibility with you that those bodies, R-1 to R-17, that is to say the bodies by the side of the canal, had been moved into the position in which you saw them shortly before you arrived, in other words the possibility that they had died elsewhere and then been moved post mortem a relatively short time before you arrived. Now, first of ail, I think I'm right in saying that as far as body R-1 is concerned, your view was that that body had indeed been moved into position post mortem; is that right? You'll find that in paragraph 188 of your 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the person found in two sacks, and that led to this opinion of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And when Professor Aleksandric gave evidence, he was asked about that body and about the others, and this is transcript 6819, line 17, where he was asked whether in respect of bodies other than R-1, there were any indications that they may have been put there post mortem, and his response was, "I could say that definitely only for body number 1. As for the other bodies I could only speculate." Can I ask you this? Would you agree that as regards the other bodies, that is to say R-2 to R-17, it is impossible to say with certainty whether they had been moved post mortem or had died at the scene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the French version, I hear that the bodies have been removed after post mortem examination. I think that might be a translation issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read the English transcript and then of course I do not know how it's translated for Professor Dunjic, could I ask you, in order to avoid whatever confusion, Mr. Emmerson, to repeat your question -- well, starting at page 31, line 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That said, the question is a very general question, bodies R-2 and R-17 are mentioned. I would be very grateful to Mr. Emmerson if he could specify and talk about each question individually rather than addressing the issue in the form of a group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an accepted technique to start with the general question. If the witness would say, for none of them, then we don't have to go one by one. If the witness says, well, perhaps for three or four, then I expect Mr. Emmerson to ask which three or four and then go into further detail. That is more efficient. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm -- just to be absolutely clear, I am working from the general statements in testimony and in the 92 ter statement at paragraph 710 that I referred to which was an overall statement about the remains collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm asking you whether you would agree, Mr. Dunjic, leaving R-1 aside that the other remains found by the side of the canal, as regards those remains, it is impossible to say with certainty whether they were moved there after death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could agree with such a statement, that it is not possible to establish with certainty, but with a high degree of probability as a possibility, I would agree that those bodies were there. Now, whether they were brought there after death or were injured on the spot is something I cannot ascertain, that is, the site of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm looking at the clock. Would it be a suitable time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we, Professor Dunjic, will have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't intend to call this week this witness. We have decided to withdraw him from the list. I agreed with Mr. Guy-Smith on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, is he withdrawn from the list or is he postponed indefinitely?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later. He's not withdrawn from the list. It's just for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and for those reasons, Mr. Guy-Smith, I take it that you would agree that your motion should be kept on hold rather than anything else at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not on the microphone but I will repeat your word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes is the answer for Mr. Guy-Smith. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Actually, it's not on the transcript which witness you were speaking of, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to cut matters short it's about Mr. Versonnen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, I think you can confirm, can you, that with the sets of remains that were recovered in the area adjacent to the canal wall, in quite a large number of instances, there were missing bones that were not recovered from the location.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact details but the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We can look at the exact details if we need to, but in the case of quite a number of bodies, there were parts of the skeleton that were missing and never recovered, and in other instances, the body had become disarticulated and separated?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that pattern consistent with bodies having been moved post mortem?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a specific answer to that question because bodies next to the concrete part of the canal were on the surface and also those in the natural part of the canal were in the water or next to the water but what I can assume is that the missing bones occurred in the case of fractures and then certain fragments went missing, which correlated to the data that we found traces of animal teeth indicates that the fact that certain body parts were missing could have been removed by animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly. One possible explanation is scavenging but would you agree that another possible explanation is that the body has been buried elsewhere, dug up and moved?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not accept such a submission because certain bodies found there next to the canal had injuries on them with firearms and blunt objects. Where the injuries caused -- were the cause of death, it is possible that the bodies were not immediately moved from the place where the injuries were suffered to the place where they were found. This is one fact. The other thing is that the bodies next to the canal were found on the surface itself, partly covered by a thin layer of earth and sometimes a thicker layer of earth. The bodies covered with a larger quantity of earth were in the area where one could see on the walls of the concrete canal the projectile effects, impacts. So this could indicate that the executions were done there and this would also mean that they were not buried somewhere else previously. And in connection with this assumption of yours, I have to say that the covering of clothing and bodies by earth was caused by the location where the bodies were, that there was fresh earth, like mud after rain, and that the bones which were put in a bag were put there together with the mud that surrounded them. After that, this bag with the bones was carried by hand to the truck and then again transported from the truck to the place where we did the autopsies. So the fact that the bones had earth on them was the result of the place where the bodies were found and not from where they were previously buried. So I cannot accept this assumption at all, especially on the basis of what we saw in situ, the position of those bodies and their location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get to the point, focus on what really is the issue. Of course, talking about possibilities, I mean perhaps unlike a jury this Chamber is well aware that if a body is found somewhere with some missing bones, that it could be that in transporting them, bones got missing. I could find another ten or 15 explanations for that. If we don't know what the explanation is. And then to ask whether it's consistent or not, Mr. Emmerson, the question should be is it consistent tore is it inconsistent with. And if you say it could be consistent, then of course, it doesn't assist the Chamber that much. That there are several explanations is clear, and in the answer you may have noticed that what you present as one of the possible explanations is then interpreted by the witness as an assumption. I didn't hear it to be put as an assumption but just as a possibility and we are close to the area of speculation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I, with that comment in mind, please, ask to you take the green file and to turn to tab 13? I just want to ask you about two sets of remains in particular, and behind tab 13 you will find Professor Lecomte's report, Mr. Dutertre has invited me to take to you specifics, so can I just take to you two specifics and then to the general conclusion? If you find tab 13, you should have an English and a French version of the report by Professor Lecomte. Now I'm working from the English version which is behind 13(B). If you look at the second pink tab there. And if you could start please at page 24, in respect of body R-13 and having viewed the photographic material and the reports, you can see in the bold type the conclusion of the team of French pathologists that that body had been dead for approximately two months but that the totality of the factors viewed at the discovery site and the information noted at post mortem led the French team to conclude that the body had been at the site only for a very short time. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I remember that Mr. Dixon didn't wish for this report to be given to Professor Dunjic so that he could comment upon it. Concerning the other witness, it was agreed that the document would be transmitted to him. Sufficient time was given to him so that he could make comments. Therefore, all this may be done in possible conditions for the whole report. I can see today that Professor Dunjic is being given just now this report which the Defence didn't wish to be given to him, without him having heard the possibility to actually read it, peruse it, this report, so I object to the use of this report today with Professor Dunjic. It was the Defence itself who hadn't wished -- I remember very well in the last day we had examined these matters -- that this report be transmitted to him for him to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm happy, if Mr. Dutertre objects, to defer this line of questioning until Professor Aleksandric returns with his report. If objection is taken to it, I'm happy to defer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, what I mean to say is that Defence had all possibilities to say that it wished to interrogate Professor Dunjic on this matter, when this was tabled about a month ago. And if it had wished to do so then the question was clearly asked by the Chamber to know whether Prosecution as Defence wished this report to be submitted to Professor Dunjic, and Defence said that it didn't wish so. This is what I remember of this exchange. So if there had been anything to be done before, it wouldn't have been needed to postpone these matters. I simply wanted to say that if these matters had to be examined in depth they should have been given beforehand to Professor Dunjic so that he could have perused it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, your point is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber considers that it does not assist if Professor Dunjic will be taken more or less by surprise, without having had an opportunity to read the general part and the specifics on a certain -- on certain remains, but then as a whole and not just conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I entirely take the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to then check whether the experts have taken the same data as a starting point for their conclusions so therefore if you would like to do this exercise with Professor Dunjic, then at least, although I hesitate, Professor Dunjic, to say that more homework would be there, but at least not do it now and that a proper opportunity should be given to Professor Dunjic to read both general part and those portions of the report you'd like to draw his attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point and since primarily Professor Aleksandric has been charged with the responsibility for preparing a further report and commenting on it, then obviously the opportunity exists for the matters to be explored with him. What I was seeking to do is simply to give this witness an opportunity to respond given the general comments that have been made in evidence-in-chief about the length of time that bodies have been at the location but I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be a solution, Mr. Dutertre, I'm also addressing you, that, Mr. Emmerson, you're not putting any further questions, I take it, Professor Dunjic, that you have a certain professional interest in getting acquainted with what other experts might have said about the report and therefore if you'd be so curious to know what's in there, if you want to read it, that you're not obstructed from doing so. And I'm now looking both at Mr. Dutertre and at all Defence counsel, whether they would oppose Mr. Dunjic, if he's interested, to read the report and to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Makes very good sense to me, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. President, no objection. For that to be complete, I think perhaps one should also give the last report, which there was a motion about it from the Prosecution on this matter concerning the translation of a new report on Rule 94 by Mr. Truel [phoen]. I see that this report actually is on the list of documents which Mr. Guy-Smith communicated to me and on which he wants to rely for his possible cross-examination. Therefore this would enable the witness to have an a complete view of all the reports which have been filed on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather delay any decision on that until the Chamber has formed an opinion about the timing and the content and the importance of that report. There are procedural aspects in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This raises another matter, Mr. Guy-Smith. There is a motion, could I say a rather short motion, not giving a lot of explanation, on the timing and the importance of this report. If you intend, and of course this was not disclosed to the Chamber, if you intend to use that report, may we interpret that as there is no objection against the introduction of that report in evidence? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The manner in which the Chamber has framed the question leaves me a moment of pause because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps -- could perhaps all three Defence counsel briefly respond. Of course, I'm not preventing you from making further submissions on it, but if there would be a clear and short answer, the Chamber would like to hear it, if possible, after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll tell you right now it was my inclination with regard to that motion to request that he be available for cross-examination at a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not opposed admission of the report itself but if similar short answers could be obtained from other counsel then the Chamber would appreciate to hear not later than today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before I move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps I address briefly Professor Dunjic. Professor Dunjic, there is a report that you've not seen. There is an English translation of that report. You'll not be taken by surprise, no questions will be put to you at this moment about it. If, however, from professional interest you'd like to read it overnight and perhaps tomorrow morning, and if would you have some comment on it, and of course that would not be, then an opportunity will be given. So I'm not saying this is your homework, but I'm saying if you want to spend your night in reading this report, it will be provided to you. But I can imagine that you would like to do other things. I don't know, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I could see, it is a voluminous report. Just by going through what was put before me concerning R-13 requires a more detailed analysis. I'm afraid I wouldn't be able to do that tonight in entirety, without referring to the original photo file and without analysing the on-site records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As regards any cross-examination that I have of this gentleman, I do not intend to cross-examine him in an area where he would be hampered or have incomplete information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not even allow you to do so, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It would not be my intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question is that we do understand that Professor Dunjic considers himself not to be able to master the content of this report overnight and therefore we will not even try to convince him to do that. Next question is: Would any party oppose of the report being provided to Professor Dunjic so that if at any later stage he would like to send a written comment on it or perhaps, together with Professor Aleksandric, formulate further responses to that, that at least he has the report available.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see no objections from Defence, no objection from you Mr. Dutertre? Professor Dunjic, you'll be provided with a report, with an English version, with no obligations attached to it but all opportunities. Please proceed. Yes, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point of clarification. Must I understand from Mr. Emmerson's head nod after what Mr. Guy-Smith said, that this would be a sign of approval and that this report should be given to Mr. Dunjic? I'm not sure we have taken a decision on this, unless I have got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about the Lecomte report and we are not-- I know Mr. Emmerson good enough by now to know that if I would have misinterpreted his nodding he would have certainly brought it to my attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before I move to the next topic I said that I would play you a short passage of videotape and I'm doing this for one specific reason, Mr. Dunjic. When I asked you to compare the photographs of those two sets of remains that we see in the blue file, in tabs 2 and 3, that is photographs D43 and D44, you made the observation that they were poor photographs from which it was difficult to see the degree of decomposition. Just to remind you, you've suggested to us that the body that's shown in photograph D43 could either be R-21 and R-24 or it could be R-29, and as we established earlier on, in respect of both of those sets of remains, the post mortem report established that the remains were skeletonised, in the case of R-21 and R-24 mostly without soft tissue and in the case of R-29 almost complete skeletonisation with no soft tissue and similarly, as far as R-18-1 and R-32 are concerned, the woman whose body was unidentified, R-18-1, I think you'll confirm, consisted of a bare skull vault with no tissue on it at all that was found at the bottom of the falls.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, with that introduction, I'd just like to play you a passage of videotape which may show those two floating bodies in a little more detail and ask to you help us as to whether your opinion is any different. This is P72, the video P72, at 4.50, that is, four minutes, 50. And it should be showing in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that's probably sufficient for the present purposes. We can stop it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I don't know whether you'd like to see that passage of video again, Mr. Dunjic, but the suggestion I make to you is that it's perfectly clear in respect of both of those bodies that they are fleshed, indeed the fingers are visible and in respect of the body with the white trousers, hair is visible. Do you agree with those propositions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All that is visible, although one can see the changes that have occurred due to putrefaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I accept that. Do you still say that the body with the light-coloured trousers is consistent with either R-21 and 24 or R-29, both of which were recorded as being skeletonised without soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to that part of the report referring to R-29.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see that for the most part, soft tissue is missing, although from the photographs one can see that parts of soft tissue are still there. However, the process of putrefaction can be speeded up if the body is out in the open and if there is water around. It can also be partially skeletonised. Therefore, if we go back to the photographs made at autopsy, as regards the body marked with 29, one can see that parts of soft tissue are preserved but that the skull and the legs are bare. These are the photographs or rather this is 29(B). That's a photograph from the autopsy. I took all of that into account, taking into account the time period that elapsed between the footage and the autopsy and the taking of the photographs. Therefore I allow for a possibility, as I've stated already, and the possibility is that these bodies may be the bodies found in the canal. This is not necessarily an assertion but a presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just finally on that score, Mr. Dunjic, if you look at 29(A) where we see again the photograph of body 29 in situ in the canal, with the bare bones appearing as they do in that photograph, would you agree that on the footage we've just seen that body had a foot which was clearly visible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not found. The bones were not found. Therefore, animals and fish, shellfish and rodents that may have been nearby, they first go for the parts of the body which are the most accessible, these being the face, hands, the skull and the feet. Therefore, I had to take that into account as well. And on top of that, there was a time during which the corpse was exposed to water.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I turn now to the subject of identification very briefly? And I want to focus on the 12 individuals who were positively identified by your commission and in respect of whom death certificates were issued. First of all, two of those remains we know were individuals who were attributed with bones that had been provided to you from Dasinovac, correct? And those individuals had been found in conjunction with identification documents; is that right? Which, if one puts those to one side, leaves us with ten sets of remains that were recovered either from the area adjacent to the concrete section of the canal or from the natural canyon that were the subject of identifications. I see you nod, if you could just confirm as we are going through, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think that you are aware that of those ten individuals, the remains of six of them were successfully exhumed and DNA comparisons carried out in order to establish whether the methodology that you had used at Hotel Pastrik had resulted in correct or incorrect identification. Is that something that you're aware of in respect of those six individuals? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in three of those instances, the identifications that had been conducted by your team at Hotel Pastrik were confirmed, but in three other cases, it turned out that the identifications were in error and you were aware of that, I think?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one or two questions an in little more detail about those three cases. First of all, R-3, I think it's right, and you say this at paragraph 121 of your 92 ter statement, that you personally took the history from a lady called Zoja Seferaj, with respect to her missing husband, Hadzi or Adzija Seferaj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
