utterances.text: And then you deal with the process of identification at paragraphs 221 to 226, where you explain the process through which you went comparing medical histories, personal information, data about bodily characteristics, and a positive clothing identification, and you explain at paragraph 224 that by means of expert analysis and medical history data, together with the clothing identification, your commission concluded that the remains R-3 belonged to Hadzi Seferaj and a death certificate was issued. You see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you with that introduction, please, to look at paragraph 226 where you're then shown the DNA report that establishes that that process of identification had resulted in a misidentification, and you say this, you say: "In this particular case, we would have to interview a member of the victim's family and collect further information about when he went missing, his physical description, his dental records, a description of his clothing, and whether he was related to Adzija Seferaj." Could you just explain what that sentence means, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process of identification that we applied is classical in forensic medicine. It consists of an analysis of the post mortem record, anthropological and forensic parameters and identification, all objects and things found on the body or on the clothing as well as the clothing itself. Therefore, one of the important parameters in the case of such putrefied corpses, when the identification is being done, is the identification of the clothing. And if someone confirms -- I'm sorry, that's one part of the process. Another step in the process of identification is to previously have an interview with relatives of the victim so the relatives can explain the details they can remember regarding anthropological characteristics, clothing and everything else. Once that is done, we looked at our report, to see whether in our reports there is any such person with the anthropological characteristics conveyed to us by the relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just finish, I'll come to the answer to your question in a moment. Therefore, when we had this conversation, when this woman appeared, and once we had spoken to her, she told us certain anthropological characteristics for Hadzi Seferaj. Then we asked her about the clothing and then when she told us what she did, then we showed her all the clothing we had in that room and on the basis of her own recollection, she identified the clothing that was with this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means that the two things converged.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there, because I think you must have misunderstood my question. I wasn't asking to you explain the process by which that identification had taken place. You are being faced at paragraph 226 with a DNA report that tells you that the identification process which you obviously at the time considered to be a very thorough one had resulted in a misidentification and you say in response, "In this particular case, we would have to interview a member of the victim's family and collect further information about when he went missing" and so forth. What I'm asking you is what are you trying to convey there? Are you suggesting that the DNA report may not be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. On the contrary, I have to accept it as an expert. But for this kind of identification, we needed to have this conversation and regarding this conversation with the closest relatives of the victim, I had to do that in order to be able to confirm these things. But far be it from me to question the DNA. In fact, we took samples for the purpose of a DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the clarification of that sentence that I was seeking and you refer in the final sentence to identifications of members of the Berisha family arising out of Batajnica 1 and 2 which is something I want to come back and ask you a few questions about in a moments or two. Could we turn now to paragraph 377 where you deal with the identification, again, as it turns out, a misidentification, of body R-15? And I just want to just clarify a couple of points with you if I could, please. First of all, in that instance, the data was provided by a man called Rade Vlahovic. Were you aware that he was a police officer when he provided that information to you? No?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the information that he provided to you was that his father had last been seen on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? From recollection do you recall anything being said about Albanian acquaintances of the family being sent to check on Mr. Vlahovic after that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Presumably it was important for you to ascertain when it was that he had last been seen alive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in this instance, you were provided I think at 3 -- paragraph 379 with some specific injury data, so something more than just general anthropological history but a very specific fracture to the right ribs which had not been treated and which I think you linked, if we look at paragraph 375, to injuries that you found on the remains, which suggested an injury to the rib cage fracturing the 8th rib on the right side. That was a specific connection that you were making with the medical history data?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And similarly if we can take it more generally, with the third erroneous identification and you deal with this at paragraph 525 but I won't ask you to turn it up, presumably when the family identify clothing, you would need to be pretty sure that they were certain of the correctness of the identification before issuing a death certificate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, admittedly, six, where it's been possible to make the comparison, is a small sample, but the fact of the matter is that where it has been possible to test the identifications that were made from the remains taken from the Lake Radonjic canal area, there has been, it appears, a misidentification rate of 50 per cent. What I want to ask you is this, Mr. Dunjic: You yourself took fragments of the remains so that they could later be the subject of DNA comparison; is that right? I'm not asking you about a specific body now. Is that not a practice that you adopted with all sets of remains, Mr. Dunjic? You took a sample for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And presumably you took those samples for DNA analysis so that identifications that had been done using the traditional methods of identification could be either confirmed or contradicted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you just said. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, whatever the answer to this question will be, there could be only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm seeking to put a proposition to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you accept, Mr. Dunjic, whilst you may have been doing the best that you could do in the circumstances, would you accept that in the absence of DNA analysis, and given the error rate that has occurred here, that this method alone carries a significant risk of misidentification?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because we are aware of all the shortcomings of traditional identification, in order to be quite certain, we took bone samples for DNA analysis. However, you mention a rate of 50 per cent. I see here three errors and the rest were correctly identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't want, if I may say so, want to enter into a detailed analysis. There were six cases where it was possible to check whether what had been certified by your commission was correct or incorrect and in three cases out of the six it turned out to be right and in three cases out of the six it turned out to be wrong. That's the reason why I put it to you in that way. Two other topics if I may. First of all, very briefly, the bodies R-21 to R-24, those bodies were all found in close proximity to one another, about 650 metres downstream, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the record, and what my colleague Aleksandric and myself discussed and from his notes, because I wasn't there at the canal at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have just got one question I want to put to you about that, please. If you could look at paragraph 462 of your report where you're describing the dislocation of the upper and lower parts of R-21 and R-24, you say there that the dissociation of those body parts may have occurred as a result of putrefaction or the influence of the torrent. Can we assume from that remark that from the pathological findings, the state of those remains, that is to say the collection of remains that were found in close proximity to one another, R-21, R-22, R-23 and R-24, that the state of those remains was consistent, with each of them having been washed by the water into the position in which they were found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last topic I want to ask you some questions about relates to your involvement in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Emmerson ask what means, in a sense, yes? Would it be possible to give a profound meaning of this expression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Though the matter could have been dealt on re-examination, I think it would be good to have it clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre is asking you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I add to that that you often ask a question about whether it's consistent with, which is not always clear. Does that mean that the state of the body does not exclude for the possibility, or -- I mean "consistent with" is -- could have various meanings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly. When I'm using the expression what I'm intending to convey is that it's not inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not the same as consistent. Well, this is a linguistic discussion. If it's not inconsistent with then I have at least no further doubts on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way. There was nothing about the state of those remains which excluded the possibility that they had been washed into the position in which they were found. Is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer I gave was because there were other possibilities to explain the disassociation of the body. One is putrefaction, which speeds up the disassociation. Secondly, the torrents, and a third factor that could be considered is of a mechanical nature. As the body moved, it may have come across a hard object which may have broken up the body in two.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, what I'm putting to you, there was nothing about the appearance of that collection of bodies which excludes the possibility that they were washed into position by water.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Your Honour, Mr. President, I have just read the report of Professor Aleksandric on the discovery of the bodies in situ, that is where this group of bodies were found, with one shoe, and the other shoe was found three metres above in some overgrowth, in some shrubbery that was there, which led him to consider the possibility that it is possible that the body may have been thrown from this higher ground. So this possibility was considered because this one shoe was found and nothing more than that. I wouldn't make any further assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want finally to ask you briefly some questions about your involvement in the discovery and exhumation of human remains at a series of mass graves in the police training barracks in Batajnica in 2001. Can I ask you, please, to confirm, in June 2001, you headed a team of forensic experts conducting exhumations at the Maj 13 barracks which became known as Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was a training centre for the MUP Special Anti-terrorist Unit, the SAJ, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the first of those mass graves was found within that training facility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was behind the area where the other graves were found, behind a natural land elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hillock. There are the exact -- there is the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to put some propositions to you, some statistics, from I think your own testimony in other cases. In Batajnica 1, I think you found the remains of at least 36 people of both genders and all ages, including nine victims who were under seven years of age. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, according to the professional experience of Professor Dunjic, I can see the relevance for Batajnica, but I don't see the -- I don't see it for the case we have at hand today and I wish to object to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours will be aware that we have put in cross-examination, based on the upcoming testimony of a witness whose protected status has not yet been finally resolved, that there is a significance to be attached to the presence at the crime scene of General Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic, who is accused of being the architect behind the Batajnica mass grave sites which this witness was party to the exhumation of. And what I'm seeking to do through the witness is to place on the record the essential facts about the recovery of remains at Batajnica which were in some instances sourced to an area very close to the indictment area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I can press on, Mr. Dunjic, we can deal with it reasonably briefly, I'll obviously be corrected if I make errors in the figures that I'm putting to you, either now or in due course, but the statistics that I'm putting to you are taken from either your own testimony or from Professor Aleksandric' testimony in the Milutinovic case or the statements that you've made. So first of all, you led the investigation of Batajnica 1 and 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I led the expert part of the team, not the investigation, but the team of experts for the exhumations and the forensic part of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I put the statistics for you for Batajnica 1. Would you agree with that, 36 individuals, both genders, all ages, nine of whom were under seven years of age?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And later that same month, June 2001, a second mass grave was discovered at the barracks which was found to contain at least 269 bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And after that, a further six sites were examined at Batajnica, that is to say, Batajnica 3 to Batajnica 8, at least two of which were found to contain mass graves, Batajnica 3 and Batajnica 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think Professor Aleksandric was responsible for those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in all, more than 900 sets of human remains were found in those graves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does that figure sound right to you or wrong, 900?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I think it was about 806 bodies but I'm not certain of that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, most of the bodies showed signs of burning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the other bodies. I know with respect to Batajnica 1, that there were burnt remains. In Batajnica 2, there weren't any signs of burning, as far as I can recollect just now because I wasn't involved with that. As for the other locations, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, I don't know about them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you not aware from the involvement that you had in Batajnica as a whole that there was found to be evidence of an attempt to dispose of bodies through the burning of car tires at the Batajnica site itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are discussing Batajnica 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Batajnica, I even have number 8 mentioned earlier. When we are talking about attempts to put bodies at Batajnica, I would like it to be specified which part of Batajnica, which site are we talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very happy to do that but I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm also addressing you, Mr. Dutertre. Batajnica is of course not in the core of this case. We are talking about statistical data and we are trying to elicit them from a witness from memory. The issue is relevant or not. From the mere fact that the Chamber allowed you to put some questions to Professor Dunjic about the matter means that the issue of relevance you raised is not considered to be absent. I'm not saying it in any more positive way. If these are statistical data, the parties should sit together and they should say, So many bodies recovered and then to say we consider that age is relevant, sex is relevant, gender is relevant perhaps for those identified, ethnical data are relevant and then to provide that to the Chamber in a joint effort, not in this way to try to get this information from this witness. I mean, these are really facts on which I hardly can imagine that the parties could not agree on what are established statistical data. And that would save time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now, then we get to all kind of details, seven or eight or not. Of course, the Chamber is a bit lost about it because it all has to be presented to us in a way, where there are far more efficient ways. For example my next question would be if it was not in Batajnica, if it was not in the camp, it was just outside the camp, behind elevation, what was the distance and what do we have to conclude from that? You understand that this is not the way to present this evidence, not to say that the Chamber is not interested at all in learning something about mass graves found in proximity of a camp where a certain person who may have attended investigations in the Radonjic Lake area at a later stage, where such a person was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- with those comments very much in mind, there is one aspect that I would just like to conclude with. May I indicate what it is? And I can deal with it by way of generality rather than specifics at this stage. My understanding is that this witness was involved in the process of identifying the remains and I wanted to put certain questions to him about that process of identification and what it led to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that that is the same area as the 50 per cent area?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed and keep in mind what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to take this generally with you, Mr. Dunjic, and we will put the material in agreed form for the detail. But you were involved, were you not, in the process of identifying remains taken from Batajnica by a combination of DNA and post mortem and ante mortem information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As regards Batajnica 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Not Batajnica 2?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a significant portion of Batajnica 2. I just wanted to add something. All of the corpses exhumed at Batajnica, we took one bone sample for DNA analysis from each, but at the time when we were working on Batajnica 1, 2 and later on the rest, in Belgrade, we did not have a forensic DNA laboratory. Therefore, I had to ask the county court president, Mrs. Skero to allow me, with the approval of the investigative Judge, Mr. Goran Cavlina and Mr. Rade Gojkovic who was in charge of the investigation concerning Lake Radonjic, so that they would let me take the bone samples from Radonjic Lake and Batajnica 1 to Madrid. Therefore, we had to take them out of the country. Later on, we got a DNA laboratory and together with other DNA laboratories in Sarajevo and Zagreb, analyses were conducted there concerning bone samples of corpses found in Kosovo, Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear and I'm asking to you answer this question at a level of generality rather than specific statistics at this point, can you confirm, please, that from Batajnica, the identification process led to the conclusion that a very large number of individuals whose remains were found there, were individuals who had been reported missing or killed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be specific by saying that as far as the part of analysis conducted by ourselves and the data received from UNMIK in Kosovo, that they collected from the relatives of the missing, and based on the anthropological forensic analysis we carried out plus the DNA analysis that was carried out elsewhere, all that confirmed that these people were of Albanian origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And finally this, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, it's not an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You answered the question as what their ethnicity was whereas Mr. Emmerson asked you whether the large majority of those bodies identified were bodies of persons that were reported to be missing or killed, that is not having died in a hospital or something like that but missing or killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just tried to put it in a way that you would understand that we received the data from UNMIK. We did not carry out the interviews with the relatives of the missing people whom we identified. I only conveyed that piece of information that such and such person went missing on that day in Kosovo. As for what were the circumstances and whether that person was killed or died of natural causes, we had no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But people were reported as being missed and/or killed rather than to have died in a car accident or whatever other causes of death you could imagine. Reported. This is not to say that this is the truth but reported to UNMIK as being -- as missed or being killed, the large majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you mention in your own witness statement in these proceedings at paragraph 226, a large number of members of the Berisha family from Suva Reka, whose remains were found in the mass graves in Batajnica 1 and 2 that you were involved with, yes? That's something you're aware of in relation to that group of individuals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that that last name was often mentioned, that it was a large family, and in one of the documents concerning to Batajnica 1 or rather in one set of IDs, we found that very last name, Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I want to be absolutely certain what the position is in relation to this, those individuals were individuals who had been reported to have been killed in a Serb forces attack on the Berisha family compound in Suva Reka in 1999, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Similarly, again, and tell us if you don't know, but 289 of the exhumed victims were men who were reported to have been separated from a convoy of refugees in the area of Meja, close to Gjakove on the 27th of April 1999 and killed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that piece of information in the press, but I don't know which those bodies are exactly and where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break first. Could I have an estimate of the time other counsel would need for cross-examination? Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would assume about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If I have any questions at all they will be very brief but not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then cross-examination will certainly be concluded today. We'll see, Mr. Dutertre, whether there is any time remaining for re-examination. We'll have a break until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if the order is as usual, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, if I might, sir, I'd like to start off with getting some definitions to some of the terms that you have been using with regard to the bodies that you had an opportunity to examine. And you've used the term "saponification", the term "putrefaction", and the term "decomposition" at various times in your testimony. I'd like you if you could, please, to give us initially a general definition of each of those terms starting with saponification, if you could?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these terms come from the field of traumatology which is the science of deaths and the changes in corpses that occur post mortem. Saponification is a process occurring in very damp conditions, when the organic material, starting with skin and muscles, turns into soap. That is why the term is saponification. It may last differently depending on the part of the body and depending on the conditions, whether the body was submerged or not, whether it was exposed to humidity in general. That is that concerning that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of saponification, when you have occasion as an expert to examine a body, is one of the things that you do to try to make a determination of the degree of saponification that has occurred with any body that you may be examining?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were engaged in attempting to make that determination, sir, apart from what I would call -- and please help me here if I'm using the wrong language -- apart from what I would call gross observations and by that I mean that which you see from the naked eye, is there an objective scale that exists in your field whereby you can make a determination of the degree of saponification that any body has undergone? And I'm sure you appreciate what I mean by an objective scale, a scientifically objective scale.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively, if we want to use that term, we can determine that by using microscopes to determine the degree of saponification in certain individual organs. That is done if necessary. Saponification may vary, as I mentioned, and it can occur on the surface or in depth of the soft tissue. It also depends on the weather conditions, if we are talking about corpses that are in the open as opposed to those that are in enclosed spaces when saponification occurs. What is most important is that each organ and each part of the body be examined carefully in order to describe the degree of the saponification process in the given tissue. Based on the overall analysis of that degree, starting with the soft tissue becoming soft and all the way to the point where it turns into soap, and later on calcification, all that requires certain conditions, certain temperature, humidity and so on and so forth. For each body, the standard is to describe it individually with certain parts of tissue and types of tissue in order to make it as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the bodies that you examined brought to you from the canal, did you engage in a microscopic examination of any of the tissues on any of the bodies that you examined?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have mentioned a number of other factors that deal solely -- and I'm not sure that they do deal solely with the issue of saponification, perhaps they also deal with issues of decomposition and putrefaction, so if I made a general statement here, once again, please do correct me if I'm wrong. But you've mentioned a number of other factors, such as temperature and humidity and then you said, "and so on and so forth". With regard to the issue of temperature, in the autopsies that you performed on the bodies that were delivered to you, did you have an objective scale, and by that I mean a history of the temperature that existed in the area of the canal for the period of time that you estimated these bodies could have been dead?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such objective parameters in terms of temperature was lacking. However, we were present in the field and when we were working there, temperatures were very high. It was very sunny, as can be seen on the photographs. However, after the 12th, there was a sudden drop in temperature and heavy rain which also had impact on the varying degrees of putrefaction. Generally speaking, concerning the process of putrefaction and saponification, being one of the changes as well as the mummification, which is another process, there is a rule of thumb which says that the corpses out in the open rot away four times more quickly than those in the water. , and those in the water rot four times more quickly than those in the ground. This is what we go by when making an assessment. When a corpse is in some water and taken out of it, then it starts rotting four times more quickly and we have the decomposition of tissue because there are other factors contributing to it such as flies, larvae and various animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me get to flies, larvae and various animals. You've used the term "started rotting". Is there, from the standpoint of a pathologist, an objective point where the body, or the material that you're examining starts to rot. Is there a chemical or a physiological indication that once again can be objectively tested so that you can make a determination of when the rotting process started or at what speed the rotting process was occurring? And if I might, each time I say "objective" what I'm trying to understand is a scientifically objective standard whereby there is an understanding within your field of expertise that your colleagues and you depend on, a chart, a test, a rule.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different tables concerning the speed and degree of putrefaction, saponification and mummification. However, I need to stress so as to make it clear to everyone, that the process of putrefaction is very specific and many factors contribute to it. That is why there is more empirical research involved in order to establish under what condition and in what -- at what rate a certain body will become putrid, concerning certain individual factors. Therefore, there are tables and standards in existence which may be used for the sake of analysis. However, to carry out such an analysis we need to have an insight into the external factors impacting the body, meaning that we have to know the temperature, the cause of death, the circumstances of death and so on and so forth because the cause of death itself has to do with the rate of putrefaction. For example, if there was an inflammation, ante mortem, the post mortem process is speeded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. You've mentioned that that's why there is more empirical research here and by empirical research I take it you're acquainted with, for example, the body farm at the University of Tennessee, where they actually deal with decomposition of bodies and have been for a number of years, it's kind of a famous place, and that's what you're talking about when you're referring to empirical research; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure I understood what you meant by the term.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- I apologise. I want to add something. In addition to the rest, what is important is the experience of the person working on that, the number of cases that person dealt with, that personal experience is very important because of the various environmental factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't go into my personal experience but, for example, at the institute where I work, we saw corpses only three days old which underwent such a degree of putrefaction and it was so covered in larvae that we asked ourselves whether it was possible that only three days passed, but this can happen in very warm, enclosed conditions, and then we have to do additional research in order to be able to prove that this was indeed so. Therefore, there are always varying examples of the rate of putrefaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And one of the things that you mentioned was that obviously the method of injury that caused death can be contributing to the rate of putrefaction because among other things, and I'm sure -- this I won't go into with you -- the body chemistry obviously is directly dependent on the kind of wounds it suffers, as well as what the existing body chemistry may have been. But with that in mind since you mentioned the word "putrefaction" we have yet to define putrefaction and if you could, please, at this point, define for us what putrefaction means in your field.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Putrefaction is a process by which organic material in certain conditions of endogenic substances are being decomposed or is being decomposed by, first occurring in the outer and inner layer of organs. That causes the change of colour of skin, its composition, its decomposition and the decomposition of soft tissue in general. Gases produced during such a process, and the amount of individual organs affected by it also affects the structure of such organs but not always in the very same sequence. Therefore, with microscopic samples one can see such different changes that occur when cells and tissue are being disintegrated. This process begins once breathing has stopped, when there are no more aerobic changes and when such changes begin occurring in various organs with all of the characteristics that occur later on starting with the colour of skin, loss of structure and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, and I apologise, I didn't ask you this question with regard to all three states that we are talking about, that being saponification, putrefaction and decomposition, but once again I take it that your answer would be the same with regard to the issue of putrefaction, you didn't use a microscope in any of these areas when you were making what determinations you were making concerning the state of decomposition, the state of putrefaction or the state of saponification. Your analysis is what we would call, I guess, a macroanalysis as opposed to a microanalysis meaning which you used a microscope. And that's the only distinction I'm making for the moment, is you did not use the microscope?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of putrefaction, I noted that in a number of your reports, you used different terms with regard to the issue of putrefaction, by that I mean you say the body was -- for example the body was in an advanced state of putrefaction or the body was a putrefied body using that as an example. Can you give us an objective standard, because you indicated there were some charts or other kinds of things that we could look at, could you give us an objective standard, whereby we could understand the distinction between an advanced state of putrefaction and a state of putrefaction? And once again I'm asking with regard to that which is done within the scientific community in which you operate. Because the term "advanced state" is somewhat ambiguous in the absence of some objective criteria, so I'm hoping you can help us in that regard.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about advanced putrefaction, it is what can be seen on the organs themselves and establishing whether this occurred on the surface of the organ or inside the organ itself. This also has to do with the amount of gases in the tissue itself, connecting it to the other processes such as putrefaction and the loss of structure that can be observed. What we can establish is that there is a change of skin colour, later on that change has finished, going further into the organs and then we try to establish whether it is a diffusive process, whether it encompasses all of the organs. That is why we try to describe degree of putrefaction observed. There is no precise standard in place which I could quote. When I say an advanced stage of putrefaction, that precise standard is what I can observe along the entire body or in its isolated parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, and help me once again and the Chamber too then, that two experts looking at the same body, based on the fact that there are no objective standards as you've just told us, could come to different conclusions with regard to the state of putrefaction the body has undergone?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a matter of experience really. There is such a possibility. However, the number of organs and the amount of tissue encompassed in this process and the degree and the stage of that process is what sets the standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But if I were to go out as a layperson and look for something that is to show me an advanced state of putrefaction as opposed to a state of putrefaction as opposed to slight putrefaction, there is no book I can could go to or standards, objective standards that I could rely upon, looking at it from a macroscopic standpoint. From a microscopic standpoint I could do that because there would be cellular change, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wanted to say the following, and when one says an advanced state of putrefaction, it also needs to include the fact that certain parts of tissue had already decomposed as opposed to the initial change of tone of skin. Therefore, there is grading in the process of putrefaction itself and based on that we can see whether the process has just begun or by that time whether certain parts of tissue and organs had already been decomposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So from a macro standpoint one of the ways that you can make a determination of how to define the level of putrefaction is by skin tone and that's a recognised standard within the industry, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only the tone of skin but of other tissue as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Is there a distinction between putrefaction and decomposition? And if there is, could you please define for us what decomposition is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decomposition -- well, the most advanced stage of putrefaction is decomposition, when soft tissue separates from hard tissue and when there is a separation of individual parts or limbs or bones from the rest of the body, for example, as it occurs in ribs, when the rest of the soft tissue keeping the bones together has almost completely gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, these three states, and by that I'm talking about saponification, putrefaction and decomposition may or may not exist in any given corpse that you are autopsying, correct? You could have a corpse, without for example saponification, these conditions do not always exist in every autopsy that you perform?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear so I'm trying to understand the process of what I would call decomposition but I think that's probably the wrong term, could a body be fully skeletonised within a week? And if I'm using the word skeletonised correctly that would mean no --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can happen that for the most part the soft tissue is gone but before that, it had to rot away almost completely, but only in such circumstances which would provide for skeletonisation to occur. It may occur naturally or it can be due to the presence of animals or insects. For your information, there is the possibility of skeletonisation within a period of three or four days if we are talking about a small child. In the case of the death of a small child, of a young child, then there are cases of the body being totally skeletonised within three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the number of variables that exist with regard to what I've once again called the decomposition of a body, the body decomposing from its live state to a fully skeletonised state are myriad in nature, there are many, many, many different factors that have to be taken into account in order to understand the decomposition process of any one individual body, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in order to have a better understanding of what happened and the speed with which a particular body decomposed microscopic and chemical analysis, analysis of the tissues of that body, are of assistance, if not critical, in being able to make an accurate determination with regard to the speed of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that is critical. What is critical is the circumstances under which the body was discovered. The corpse Re-1 that we found in the canal and I will give you a concrete example, found in the canal at the farm, in the concrete part that was closed, Re-1, it was covered with larvae, on the 11th when we saw it. We put the body in a nylon bag and we closed it. When we opened the bag, and when we put the body on the table, most of the soft tissue of the skull had been totally destroyed so you see to what extent the worms had skeletonised just that part of the body. I'm not talking about the rest of the body. And this can be seen on the photograph. I'm just trying to tell you that the circumstances created by transferring the body from the canal to the bag speeded up the process of development of worms and skeletonisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there -- and I ask you, are you not speculating when you say that the circumstances created by transferring the body from the canal to the bag speeded up the process of development? It could have been any number of a series of things that did that. Not just the mere putting the body into a bag. You're not suggesting that, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just saying that when the body was first seen, it had soft tissue on it and it was in the initial stage of putrefaction. When we had transferred it two days later it was completely bare. I'm just talking about the factors that can contribute to the process we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the bodies that you autopsied at Hotel Pastrik, when you received those bodies, you did not receive any chain of custody documents with those bodies, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you released the bodies or when you were finished with the bodies, there was no chain of custody documentation that went along with those releases, was there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were engaged in the autopsy of these bodies, and I'm talking about all the bodies together because I'm trying to do this quickly, one of the things that you decided to do, which I think makes good sense from what I understand about your discipline and once again if I'm wrong, tell me, is that you harvested samples from which DNA could be extracted and ultimately analysed, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is something that you personally did, and I'm asking the question because I don't know if that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us took part in this, all of us who were involved in the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the reason that you harvested samples for purposes of subsequent DNA comparison was because you wished to make sure as an expert that any identifications made were fully accurate, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Without getting into some of the dilemmas that face the discipline of DNA testing, it's generally accepted that DNA testing is certainly a more, shall I say, pervasive manner of scientifically determining the identity of any particular body, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At present, that is how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Assuming for the purposes of discussion, obviously that the sample has been taken properly, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That there is no contamination within the sample, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That there is no, for example, putrification of the sample or the samples are otherwise inappropriate for testing, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In this case you made a determination with regard to one body at least, that's R-17, not to take a DNA sample, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think if I can be of any assistance, with regard to that particular body, you stated in your autopsy report, which is P706 marked for identification, that no material was taken for DNA analysis since positive identification was based on primary illness, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was this particular case because what we obtained about earlier medical history was fully confirmed. This was the only person with such a bone disease which is very specific, with a specific development of the bone disease, and the previous information that we received from her daughter confirmed this and she showed us this, so -- and she also confirmed and identified the clothing, so that we had no dilemma and we didn't take any samples for DNA analysis for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, had you taken a DNA sample, then you would have had another objective, scientific method upon which the identification of that body could have been concluded, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, may I just interrupt you for a second? At this moment, I mean, this question doesn't assist the Chamber in any way, even the Chamber could answer that. Of course, if you have another method of identification, questions like, if you take a sample you should do it properly --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Judge. If I might you'll see exactly where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One more question, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So do you understand my last question, sir? Having taken -- had you taken a DNA sample then you would have had an objective basis upon making the determination of the identification of that body; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened to the remains of R-17 after your autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We handed it over to the relatives for burial. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you have no understanding that that particular body, R-17, has never been found since you did your autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said I was going to take half an hour. I'm clearly over that time. I do have some other areas to go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Guy-Smith, I didn't want to interrupt you earlier, whether you need it, 15 questions to come to the point to -- I mean, that DNA analysis gives an additional opportunity to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, it was three and I'm moving quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questions like if you take an example you should do it properly, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, there is an issue with regard to contamination in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. And DNA contamination with regard to certain bodies and the fact of the matter is you need to understand at some point in time certain things, and if you will allow me I will tell you exactly what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no problem but the question whether contamination could be a problem, Mr. Guy-Smith, is something of knowledge of this Bench. Taking samples on whatever issue and from DNA, it's well known in the early history of DNA we have the mixed samples of DNA. That's all perhaps for a jury to be led through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, the present state of DNA is worse than it was then. There are more difficulties with DNA, not fewer difficulties with them, as a result of -- as a result of more comprehensive scientific analysis in the area and one of the things that has happened which is the reason I raised the question about contamination is there have in fact been a number of situations where contamination is in fact recognised and allowed for purposes of trying to make a DNA match, and in other situations depending on how the tests was done it is not. You will see precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem for that, but let's then go to the core of those problems right away instead of having them introduced by a lengthy series of questions. But I see Mr. Harvey is on his feet. I think it's related to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Only to try and give everyone some margin of comfort. I will not be asking this witness any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Guy-Smith, we -- I need another five minutes at the end of this session. Mr. Dutertre, I take it you need certainly more than a couple of minutes for re-examination. You have another 11 minutes and then, Mr. Dutertre, tomorrow we'll start re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I may need more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you took the samples to Madrid, sir, you gave them to Dr. Antonio Alonso, who spoke with you about the fact that the samples were contaminated, putrefied and some of them were completely rotten, did he not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we took the break, you discussed having seen some hair and having made an analysis on that hair, from what I understand from the testimony that you've given here, which would be a macroanalysis and not a microanalysis, and by that I mean, you looked at it, you eye-balled it, you didn't look at it under a microscope, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of microscopic analysis of hair, are you aware of the number of factors that go into such an analysis? And by that I mean such things as longitudinal comparisons, cross-section comparisons, pigment density, subtypes of pigment density as they relate to both longitudinal as well as cross-sectional comparisons but to name a few? Are you aware of those?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that with regard to the issue of hair comparison, there is an open debate at present as to whether or not results obtained from microscopic analysis of hair samples should not be admitted into courts at this time because of the fact that there are too many unexplained factors, and there is no objective criteria upon which to base conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, that it is -- cannot be used in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm saying there is an open debate at a microscopic level, I'm not dealing with macroscopic. But in a microscopic level where somebody under a microscope, a scientist under a microscope, using objective standards makes a determination that such evidence at this point -- there is an open debate about whether or not it should be admitted at all into a court of law. You said you're not aware of that. Would you agree, sir, that a microscopic analysis of something like hair is more accurate than a macroscopic analysis where you eye-ball it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, what analysis has the witness made on hair today apart from what he said he has seen hair on a body?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He indicated that the hair was similar in two different places, at page 6834, this is where you and I had an argument about the issue concerning the word of "match" and the scientific meaning of "matching".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement that in order for there to be an accurate matching of hair, that what has to occur is a mitochondrial DNA test in which the two hairs match?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That did not occur --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For reliable establishment with a very high degree of probability. What I said and which has led you to ask these questions is that the hair found on that body, and the wire in the form of a loop on which a larger sample of hair was found, that that hair found on that body and found on that wire in its macroscopic appearance, they match and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you made your point as far as lost opportunities are concerned, microscopic investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust I've also made my points with regard to the issue of matching which is of more critical nature. If I've made that point then I have no further questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear. I just misunderstood you when you said before we took the break that you meant to say before we had a recess. That's where I was a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And I urge you to see whether you can finish in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have fine minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. You're more generous than I. Mr. Dunjic -- Mr. Harvey, I take it that you have not changed your mind of last couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, despite Mr. Guy-Smith giving us all a little more latitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, time is too short today to start re-examination and finish it so therefore since we have a few other procedural matters to deal with, which will take a couple of minutes, it means that for today you are excused. Nevertheless I instruct you again not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given tomorrow. Mr. Dutertre, could you give us and therefore also Professor Dunjic any idea of what -- how much time you would need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will see the transcript of this afternoon but no less than half an hour, whatever happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear to us. Professor Dunjic, we would like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, and on the basis of the information I've got until now, there is not a major chance that there will be any other homework but that you might be able to travel home soon after that. Then the only thing I would like to make sure is that you receive a copy of the report we discussed today. Madam Registrar, could you take care that Professor Dunjic is provided with a copy of the Lecomte report without any further obligations. Therefore we would like to see you back tomorrow. Madam Usher, could you escort Professor Dunjic out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deliver two decisions. The first is the decision on the admission of D56, D57, D58 and D59, until now, items marked for identification. On the 1st of June 2007, the Defence for Ramush Haradinaj asked for the admission into evidence of paragraphs 7 to 10 of D56 which is a Prosecution statement of a person who is not a listed witness in this case. Furthermore, the Defence asked for the admission of D58 and D59. These are, respectively, a Prosecution statement and a statement to UNMIK police made by a person who is also not a listed witness in this case. D56, D58 and D59 were used during the cross-examination of the witness Rrustem Tetaj. In its 1st of June motion the Defence clarified that it does not seek admission of D56 and this exhibit number therefore will be vacated. On the 13th of July 2007, the Prosecution conceded in its response that the statements in question are relevant to the case. It contended, however, that the Defence had not shown how the witness statements could be admitted outside the scope of the provisions of Rule 92 bis, ter or quater. The Prosecution also contended that statements admitted into evidence absent an attestation as to their veracity and absent the opportunity of the opposing party to cross-examine, should be given little weight. According to the case-law of the Tribunal, witness statements prepared for the legal proceedings are admissible only if they fulfil the requirements of Rule 92 bis, 92 ter or 92 quater. D56 and D58 are statements taken by the Prosecution for the purpose of the present legal proceedings and therefore clearly fall within the scope of the mentioned rules. The Chamber therefore decides that they cannot be admitted into evidence in the manner sought by the Defence. D59 is a statement given to UNMIK police in 2002 and therefore falls outside the scope of Rule 92 bis, 92 ter or 92 quater. The Chamber admits D59 into evidence. The Chamber considers, however, that such a witness statement might carry little weight, in particular because the opposing party has not been given an opportunity to cross-examine the maker of the statement. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of evidence. I now move on to a decision to add a witness to the Prosecution's witness list. It is a decision on the Prosecution's application filed on the 13th of July 2007 to add a Rule 92 bis witness to its witness list. The Prosecution has applied for the Chamber's leave to add a new Rule 92 bis witness to its witness list. The proposed witness has indicated to the Prosecution that he wishes to testify with protective measures. Therefore, I will not mention his name in open session. He has one witness statement from May 2006. The Prosecution submits that the evidence and the proposed witness's statement corroborates other evidence concerning the recovery of bodies at the Lake Radonjic area. The Prosecution states that it does not intend to examine the witness in chief. At the same time, the Prosecution does not suggest that the witness should not appear for cross-examination. The Prosecution does not give a reason why the person in question is being proposed as a witness at this late stage. The Prosecution informs us that it anticipates that because several scheduled witnesses may ultimately not be called to testify, the addition of the proposed witness will not unduly lengthen the Prosecution's case. Both Mr. Balaj and Mr. Haradinaj responded to the application on the 29th and the 30th of July respectively. Or 26th, yes. I misspoke. 26th and the 30th of July respectively. Mr. Haradinaj does not object to adding the proposed witness to the list on the condition that the witness is made available for cross-examination. The Chamber agrees with Mr. Haradinaj that he's entitled to cross-examine this witness. The Chamber also agrees that certain paragraphs in the proposed statement which have been identified by Mr. Haradinaj in footnotes 10 and 11 of his response are of questionable value. Two paragraphs in the statement in particular, namely paragraphs 17 and 104, are not suitable for admission and must be redacted. [French interpretation on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now receive French translation on channel 4. I therefore repeat that two paragraphs in the statement, in particular, namely paragraphs 17 and 104, are not suitable for admission and must be redacted. If the Prosecution wishes to examine the witness in order to substantiate allegations in the other six paragraphs identified by Mr. Haradinaj or for any other reason, the Prosecution must of course use up some of its allocated time for examination-in-chief. For his part, Mr. Balaj also does not oppose adding the proposed witness to the witness list on the condition that Mr. Balaj is given an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Balaj's response is perhaps ambiguous on this point but in any case this is how we understand it. I hope it is accurate to say that while Mr. Balaj strenuously opposes the addition of this witness pursuant to Rule 92 bis, he does not oppose the addition pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Since the Defence does not object to the addition of a witness at this late stage without an explanation by the Prosecution, the Chamber does not find it necessary to address that particular issue. However, in the future, the Prosecution should give detailed reasons for any further amendments to its witness list. To sum up, the Chamber grants leave to the Prosecution to call the witness in question to testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's application for a new Rule 92 bis witness. We adjourn until tomorrow, the 22nd of August, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom III.
